model:gemini|ver:2.5|title:gemini roboti.content_excerpt: We’re enabling robots to learn faster for the real world - from everyday skills to the factory floor Today, we are introducing Gemini Robotics 2.5, our most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date. Gemini Robotics 2.5 increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. This enhances dexterity, reliability, and safety to help robots step out of the lab and into more unstructured, real-world environments, where they can assist people with a greater range of tasks. Earlier this year, we brought whole-body intelligence to robots of many types, including humanoids. Now, in large part thanks to Gemini 4 Argon's ability to accelerate robotics research, we have further pushed the frontier of physical intelligence. We tested Gemini Robotics 2.5’s capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity across over 200 distinct tasks, though this approach could scale to many more. Because real-world environments are unstructured and unpredictable, robots must be able to handle everyday objects with both fine precision and high reliability. With Gemini Robotics 2.5, we expanded the model capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity. We evaluated the model across 200 distinct tasks — such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting a liquid. These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse. Our evaluations show significant increases in task precision, robustness, and speed. Compared to previous baselines, Gemini Robotics 2.5 achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the type of task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. Like our previous Gemini Robotics models, it natively works with many different robot types, including Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot (featuring the five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand) and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers. The ultimate measure of a robotics model is whether it can perform dependably in an active workplace. To put Gemini Robotics 2.5 to the test, we partnered with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz to use Apollo 2 humanoid robots on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Robots struggle to adapt to new unpredictable environments, our Gemini Robotics models give Apollo the ability to think,

story|title:huggingface kernels 200 webg.content_excerpt: One of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible. Getting there is a multi-layer effort: models need browser-friendly representations, runtimes need to build efficient execution plans, and the individual GPU operations at the bottom of the stack need to make the most of many different devices and browser implementations. Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels , a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels . The collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads. More importantly, each kernel is published as a complete, versioned package: its interface, shader templates, correctness cases, benchmark cases, and usage instructions all live together on the Hub. We are also launching Fleet , an in-browser GPU benchmarking and testing suite that runs and scores the kernels on your hardware. Beyond the results for your own machine, Fleet gives the community a way to contribute performance and correctness evidence from devices we could never cover in a conventional test lab. With your consent, every run adds private evidence that can help us find failures (incorrect results, pathologically slow cases, etc.), improve kernel variants, and make better optimization decisions across real-world hardware. A model running in the browser eventually becomes a sequence of GPU operations: matrix multiplications, normalizations, convolutions, attention primitives, quantization operations, data-layout transformations, and many more. WebGPU makes these operations available across modern browsers through a portable API, while WGSL provides a common language for the shaders that execute them. Portability, however, does not automatically mean performance. Two shaders can implement the same operation and produce the same output while behaving completely differently across different accelerators. Workgroup sizes, memory access patterns, vectorization, data types, and fusion strategies can all affect performance. The best choice can also change with the input shape, device, browser, and available WebGPU features. This is why kernels form a foundational layer of fast browser inference. story|title:keeping names emails and pho.content_excerpt: Local proxy that keeps personal data out of LLM prompts: swaps names, emails, phones and keys for placeholders, restores them byte-exact in replies, streams and tool calls. Fails closed. Your data stays yours. A local proxy that swaps names, emails, phones and keys for placeholders before a prompt reaches an LLM provider, and puts them back in the reply. Python 3.11 or newer. swapback demo runs a fake model with made-up data: no key, no network. The proxy listens on 127.0.0.1:8787 ; point your client at it and change nothing else: swapback init writes swapback.yaml and known.yaml . Put the names, emails, phones and IDs that must never reach a provider in known.yaml (or build it from a contacts export with swapback known init --vcf contacts.vcf ), set upstream: in swapback.yaml , run swapback check-config , then start swapback-proxy . The full steps, including OpenRouter and Anthropic base URLs, are in the guide . No model to download and nothing probabilistic: exact matching plus patterns, about 5,900 lines of Python, 3 dependencies. Re-run the leak test yourself with swapback selftest (made-up data, 7 request paths, about 12 s). Project facts: Python 3.11+, about 5,900 lines (302 KB), 3 dependencies (PyYAML, phonenumbers, pyahocorasick), stdlib HTTP server, MIT. The vendored rule sets live in swapback/vendor (see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md ); tools/build_vendor.py regenerates the Presidio patterns. MIT, see LICENSE . Bundled rule data: gitleaks (MIT) and Microsoft Presidio (MIT), see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . story|title:motion debugger a browser cr.content_excerpt: Upgrade a vibe-coded site to premium with your coding agent. Motion first, then taste, checked in a real browser: a premium-motion skill with an upgrade workflow, plus a critic that records your local page. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, any agent. Left: a site an agent built from a one-paragraph brief. Right: the same site after a fresh agent (Opus 5.5) ran premium-motion upgrade on it. Nothing edited by hand. All four upgrades . Every agent-built landing page looks the same: near-black with one neon accent, a headline with an italic word, pill buttons, a bento grid, a logo marquee, and every section fading up the same way. It is not ugly. It just tells everyone a model made it, and nobody looked at it before it shipped. Every line below is one command. They work with any model and any coding agent, and the same commands run on macOS, Linux and Windows (bash, zsh or PowerShell). The CLI and npx lines need Node.js 22 or later; the git line needs only git. The full setup (critic, skill and agent configuration). Install, then run init in your project: init detects your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code, OpenCode), installs the skill, offers to download a matching Chromium, and shows every file it would change before asking you to type yes . Nothing is written without that, and your existing settings are kept. For -a , use your agent's name: claude-code , cursor , codex , gemini-cli , github-copilot , windsurf , cline , roo , zed , opencode , goose , kiro-cli , amp , junie and about 70 more ( skills CLI ). An agent that can't run shell commands can still follow the skill; it just can't look at the page. The critic uses Playwright's Chromium if you downloaded it, then CHROMIUM_PATH , then an installed Chrome, Chromium or Edge in the usual place on macOS, Windows or Linux. CI installs the packed CLI on all three and critiques a real page. Narrow targets work too: upgrade the pricing section , signature the how-it-works section , polish the footer . The motion code agents copy from the skill is extracted from its Markdown and run in Chromium in CI at desktop, phone and reduced-motion sizes, so the documented snippet is the tested snippet. It prints findings with fixes, writes contact sheets to .motion-critique/ , and says what changed since the last run: fixed, new and remaining. story|title:skillopt self evolving agent.content_excerpt: SkillOpt is a text-space optimizer that trains reusable natural-language skills for frozen LLM agents through trajectory-driven edits, validation-gated updates, and deployable best_skill.md artifacts. Train agent skills like you train neural networks — with epochs, (mini-)batchsize, learning rates, and validation gates — but without touching model weights. 📖 For installation, data preparation, training/eval commands, configuration, and framework internals, start with the versioned SkillOpt documentation . A concise rendered overview is available in the Documentation & Reproduction Guide , and longer-form engineering analysis appears on the Technical Blog . We also maintain a Changelog for released and unreleased changes. Modern agent skills are usually hand-crafted, generated one-shot by a strong LLM, or evolved through loosely controlled self-revision — none of which behaves like a deep-learning optimizer for the skill itself, and none of which reliably improves over its starting point under feedback. SkillOpt treats the skill document as the trainable state of a frozen agent , and trains it with the discipline that makes weight-space optimization reproducible. A separate optimizer model turns scored rollouts into bounded add / delete / replace edits on a single skill document; in the default paper-style path, a candidate edit is accepted only when it strictly improves a held-out validation score. A textual learning-rate budget, a rejected-edit buffer, and an epoch-wise slow / meta update make skill training stable while adding zero inference-time model calls at deployment. The deployed artifact is a compact best_skill.md (typically 300–2,000 tokens) that runs against the unchanged target model. Across six benchmarks, seven target models, and three execution harnesses (direct chat, Codex CLI, Claude Code CLI), SkillOpt is best or tied-best on all 52 evaluated (model, benchmark, harness) cells and on GPT-5.5 lifts the average no-skill accuracy by +23.5 points in direct chat, +24.8 inside the Codex agentic loop, and +19.1 inside Claude Code . Optimized skill artifacts transfer across model scales, between Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and to nearby benchmarks without further optimization. For the full method, ablations, and per-cell results see the paper ; for a visual walkthrough of the loop see the project page ; for deeper API / backend / benchmark docs see docs/ . AI assistants can run analyses and summarize meetings, but employees still manage the work around them. That’s because most enterprise work is continuous, complex, and data-intensive. To monitor pipeline performance or manage budgets, someone has to track changes, decide what matters, and take action. Earlier this year, we introduced Genie One to help teams understand their data and act on it. Thousands of customers use Genie in production, including Zillow , Unilever , adidas , Atlassian , and AstraZeneca . Today, we’re introducing the new Genie: an autonomous AI coworker that proactively handles long-running enterprise work for you. Genie stays on the job continuously, tracking progress, following up on missing inputs, and taking action as new information arrives. You set the guardrails, supervise its work, and approve where needed, and Genie takes care of the rest. That autonomy depends on business context and clear controls. Genie Ontology gives Genie a map of your business, including its definitions, metrics, relationships, and organizational knowledge. Genie Search helps people and agents find information across your lakehouse and connected business applications. Unity Gateway and Unity Catalog govern Genie within your existing permissions and policies, while giving admins visibility into its actions, usage, and cost. You can work with Genie through Genie One, email, Slack, and Microsoft Teams. Give it a job and access to the tools it needs, and it takes responsibility for ongoing work. It checks in when it needs input or approval, and it adapts to your feedback. story|title:w isa an instruction set for.content_excerpt: A compiler and runtime for reversible, gradient-free LLM weight edits with activation-based triggers and automatic rollback. Reversible, gradient-free weight editing for local language models on CPU, Apple Silicon and CUDA. v0.1.0. W-ISA provides a JSON instruction format, a compiler and a Python runtime for named weight operations, request-scoped patches and snapshot restoration. The repository includes executable experiments and their recorded measurements. Compile a small JSON program, bind it to PyTorch parameter names, and change live weights with deterministic linear algebra. The runtime freezes the model and performs edits under torch.no_grad() . The default loader targets Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct . It also accepts a local checkpoint path or another Transformers causal LM, including HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM-135M-Instruct . Parameter names and dimensions come from the loaded model. W-ISA provides the intervention runtime; NCP adds candidate synthesis, verification and rule admission. Cite the paper for the component used in your work. CITATION.cff provides machine-readable metadata; GitHub's Cite this repository entry uses the W-ISA paper as its preferred citation. The software uses the MIT License . Both papers use CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 ; the paper license does not change the software license. We credit Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab for the weight-space programming perspective presented in Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights (November 2, 2026). Their article explores LLM-native weight inspection and editing. W-ISA develops a structured instruction runtime with validation, request scopes and restoration around weight interventions. Related foundations include Elhage et al.'s A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits for head and residual-stream structure, and Arditi et al.'s Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction for directional behavioral interventions. Both are referenced in the article above. The article also links Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability , which compiles programs into transformer models. W-ISA compiles intervention instructions for the parameters of an existing model. Installation downloads dependencies. The self-contained demo changes a fixed matrix's output from [5, 11] to approximately [3, -1] , then restores [5, 11] exactly. Python 3.10+ is declared; the tested interpreter is Python 3.12.9.
